title: Buy Before You Sell: Bridge Loans and Other Options
description: Want to buy your next home before selling your current one? Compare bridge loans, HELOCs, contingent offers, and other ways move-up buyers make the timing work.
image_alt: A hand holding a key above small model houses

faq.a: A bridge loan is short-term financing secured by your current home that helps fund the down payment on your next home before your current one sells.

faq.q: Can I qualify for two mortgage payments at once?
faq.a: Sometimes. Lenders may count both payments, though some programs offer ways to exclude the current home's payment under certain conditions. It depends on your income, equity, and the program.

faq.q: Is a home sale contingency a bad idea?
faq.a: Not always, but it can make your offer less competitive. It works best in slower markets or when the seller has flexibility.

body_html:
For move-up buyers, timing is the hardest part. You need the equity in your current home to buy the next one, but selling first can mean moving twice, renting short-term, or rushing into a purchase. Buying first means carrying two homes, at least for a while.

There are several ways to bridge that gap. Each has trade-offs.

Option 1: Sell first, then buy

The simplest financially. You know exactly how much equity you have, and you avoid two payments. The downside is logistics: you may need temporary housing or a rent-back from your buyer. In California, negotiating a seller rent-back of a few weeks can buy time to close on your next home.

Option 2: A home sale contingency

You make an offer on the new home contingent on selling your current one. It protects you from owning two homes, but sellers in competitive markets often prefer offers without contingencies. It tends to work best in slower markets or with sellers who have flexibility of their own.

Option 3: Tap equity before you list

A HELOC on your current home, opened before you list it, can provide funds for the next down payment. Once your current home sells, the HELOC is paid off from the proceeds. Timing matters: many lenders won't open a HELOC on a home that's already listed for sale.

Option 4: A bridge loan

A bridge loan is short-term financing secured by your current home, designed specifically for this situation. It provides the funds for your next purchase and is repaid when your current home sells. Bridge loans typically cost more than long-term financing and have shorter terms, so they work best when you're confident the current home will sell in a reasonable time frame.

Comparing the options

OptionStrengthTrade-off
Sell firstSimplest, known equityTemporary housing or rent-back needed
Sale contingencyAvoids two homesWeaker offer in competitive markets
HELOC before listingFlexible, often lower costMust be opened before you list
Bridge loanBuilt for this purposeHigher cost, short term
Keep the current homePotential rental incomeTwo mortgages and landlord duties

Qualifying for two homes

If you'll own both homes at once, even briefly, lenders usually need to account for both payments in your debt-to-income ratio. Some programs allow the current home's payment to be excluded under specific conditions, such as a fully executed sale contract or documented equity and a lease. The rules are detailed, so this is a conversation to have before you write an offer.

Keeping the current home as a rental

Some move-up buyers decide to keep their current home and rent it out. Rental income may help you qualify, depending on lease documentation and program rules. If you go this route, consider landlord insurance, property management, and the tax implications. My post on DSCR loans covers financing for investors who plan to grow from there.

A sensible sequence for move-up buyers

  1. Get a realistic estimate of your current home's value and your equity
  2. Talk with your loan officer about qualifying with both payments
  3. Decide on your bridge strategy before you start touring seriously
  4. If using a HELOC, open it before listing
  5. Coordinate timelines between your listing agent, buying agent, and lender
The best move-up plans are made before the first showing, not after you find the house.

Coordinating two transactions at once

When you're buying and selling at the same time, communication becomes everything. Make sure your listing agent, buyer's agent, both escrow officers, and your loan officer all know the plan and the key dates. Ask your listing agent about negotiating a rent-back or a closing date that lines up with your purchase, and ask your loan officer how much time the new loan needs after the sale funds. A shared timeline, even a simple one, prevents the most common problems: missed contingency deadlines and sale proceeds that arrive a day too late.

Questions to answer before you start touring

  1. What is my current home realistically worth today, and how quickly do similar homes sell?
  2. How much equity will I have after paying off my current loan and selling costs?
  3. Can I qualify carrying both payments, and for how long?
  4. Would I rather move twice or carry two homes for a few months?
  5. If my current home took longer to sell than expected, what's my backup plan?

Answering these early turns a stressful juggling act into a plan. It also helps your agents write stronger offers, because they'll know exactly what terms you can commit to. In competitive neighborhoods, a buyer with a clear financing plan for the departing home often stands out from buyers who are still figuring it out.

Finally, remember that the best strategy can change with the market. In a fast seller's market, buying first with equity or a bridge loan may be the only way to compete. In a slower market, a contingent offer or a sell-first approach may cost you very little.

The takeaway

Buying before you sell is possible with the right plan. Sell first if you can handle temporary housing; use equity before listing or a bridge loan if you need to buy first; and run the numbers on carrying both homes. A quick planning call with your agent and loan officer can save months of stress and help you make a stronger offer on the home you really want.
